o: No palindrome of length 2 or 3 can exist (any longer palindrome contains one of those), so each character just needs to differ from the previous two. To get the smallest beautiful string greater than s: try to increment positions from the right; at position i, pick the smallest allowed character strictly greater than s[i] that differs from s[i-1] and s[i-2]; if found, fill the suffix greedily with 'a' unless it clashes with the previous two characters. If no position can be incremented, return "". Example "abcz": z→a fails against nothing ahead but position 3 has no larger valid char... actually 'z' is the largest, so move to position 2: 'c'→'d' works, then fill 'a' → "abda".
k: Avoiding palindromes of length 2 and 3 suffices to make the whole string palindrome-free.
Increment from the rightmost possible position, then greedily minimize the suffix.
With k >= 4, a valid filler always exists locally (at most 2 forbidden letters among 4+).

a.i: Scan i from n-1 down; attempt each character larger than s[i] that avoids the previous two; on success fill the remainder minimally.
s: For i from n-1 down to 0: for c from s[i]+1 to 'a'+k-1: if c != s[i-1] and c != s[i-2], fix prefix and go to fill step.
Fill positions i+1..n-1 with the smallest letter not equal to either of the two preceding characters.
a.t: O(26n) — at most 26 candidate characters per position during increment and fill

w: The crucial observation is that forbidding palindromes of length 2 and 3 is sufficient. Greedy fill is safe because k >= 4 guarantees a choice among any two forbidden letters. Pitfall: the increment loop must consider characters strictly greater than s[i] AND valid against the untouched prefix. Follow-up: k-th lexicographic successor, requiring counting arguments.
